paper_title: Open Vision Banana: An Open Framework for Unified Visual Perception through Generation in RGB Space

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Vision Banana showed that a closed image generator, instruction-tuned to paint perception outputs as RGB images, becomes a generalist vision model. Does this carry over to \emph{open} generators, and if not, what fails? We answer with \textbf{Open Vision Banana (OVB)}, an open framework that adapts the 7B diffusion generator of Qwen-Image-2.1 into one instruction-driven model for metric depth, semantic, instance, and referring segmentation, using a single shared low-rank adapter and public data. Each task is a \emph{task contract} whose RGB encoder, instruction, and decoder share one specification and are checked before training. Studying 42 externally evaluated checkpoints from two 100k-update runs, six exact weight-space merges, and eight controlled shorter runs, we find that the gap to the closed system is specific and measurable. Geometry is learned early while absolute scale is not: median-aligned NYUv2 $δ_1$ stays at 0.89--0.93 throughout training as unaligned $δ_1$ wanders between 0.11 and 0.50. The scale is not committed by a single sample: a ten-seed ensemble lifts unaligned $δ_1$ from 0.348 to 0.516 without retraining. Depth and 2D segmentation compete for the shared adapter, and weight merging moves along this trade-off without escaping it. Finally, lower validation flow loss comes with lower Cityscapes accuracy (Spearman $ρ\approx-0.9$ between loss reduction and mIoU), so the loss cannot select checkpoints. We release code, contracts, training data, and all evaluation outputs.

sections.title:
1 Introduction
Can one image generator, guided only by a task instruction, see depth, classes, instances, and referred objects?
Generative pretraining makes this plausible: to synthesize realistic scenes, a generator must model appearance,
object structure, and spatial layout. Marigold [18] showed that a diffusion prior transfers to monocular
depth, and Vision Banana [10] went much further:
it paints segmentation, depth, and normals as RGB
images, instruction-tunes an image generator on them, and reports results on par with specialist models while
preserving image synthesis. Image generation may thus become a general interface for perception.
sections.content: The evidence for this paradigm, however, rests on closed generator (Nano Banana Pro) trained on in-house data, with neither weights nor evaluation tools released. Two questions are therefore open: does the paradigm carry over to open generators, and, if it falls short, where exactly does it fail, and why? We argue that the second question is the more useful one. reproduction that matches number tells the community little; measured account of the failure modes tells the next model what to fix. We address both with Open Vision Banana (OVB) (Figure 1), an open, independent framework that # Corresponding author. 1 Open Vision Banana realizes the paradigm on Qwen-Image-2.1 [40, 44]a unified generation-and-editing model whose 7B diffusion transformer is conditioned by frozen 8B vision-language encoderusing public data. Building it first exposes an engineering obstacle that silently breaks generative perception: RGB is only carrier, and prediction is meaningful only if the target encoder, the instruction, and the decoder agree on units, color codes, and mask conventions. When they disagree, the training loss still decreases while the decoded predictions fail as whole. OVB therefore writes every task as task contract that derives encoder, instruction, and decoder from one specification and checks them before training. frozen editing backbone with one shared low-rank adapter then serves all tasks, selected only by the instruction. The open setting lets us study the paradigm at granularity that closed system does not allow: two 100k-update runs that differ only in learning rate, with 42 checkpoints scored on six benchmarks by an external suite; six exact weight-space merges of these checkpoints; and eight shorter runs that vary the starting point, the task mixture, the depth colormap, and the adaptation mode. OVB stays below the closed reference on every benchmark  (Table 2)  , but the shortfall is neither uniform nor mysterious. It decomposes into five findings: Geometry is learned, scale is not. Median-aligned depth is near the reference from early on; almost all of the depth gap is one number per image (Sec. 5.1). The scale is not committed. The same input yields different scales under different noise; seed ensemble recovers much of the gap without retraining (Sec. 5.2). Tasks compete for one adapter. Depth improves while Cityscapes and ReasonSeg decline, along training and across mixtures and learning rates; full fine-tuning erases referring ability (Sec. 5.3). Merging does not escape the trade-off. Exact merges move along it; only semantic segmentation gains beyond interpolation (Sec. 5.4). The training loss is blind to what fails. Validation flow loss falls while Cityscapes accuracy falls with it (Sec. 5.5). In summary, we contribute: 1. An open framework for generation-as-perception: the Vision Banana paradigm on public editing backbone with one shared adapter for four tasks, made reliable by task contracts that are checked before training. 2. diagnostic study that locates the gap to the closed system in absolute depth scale, sampling variance, and task competition under shared adapter, with every claim backed by full-benchmark external evaluation. 3. reproducible baseline: code, contracts, the 295,505-row referring-segmentation training pool, leakage-audited evaluation protocols, and every evaluation output with checksums, with all deviations from the reference protocol documented.

sections.title:
2 Related Work
Generalist vision interfaces. Painter [36] casts dense prediction as image inpainting with in-context examples.
InstructCV [11] and InstructDiffusion [13] instruction-tune text-to-image diffusion models to emit task outputs
as images, building on the editing interface of InstructPix2Pix [3]. Vision Banana [10] scales this idea to a
strong closed generator and reports specialist-level results, and related studies find emergent perception in
image and video generators [38, 45]. OVB follows the RGB formulation of Vision Banana on public models
and data; everything the paper does not disclose (adapter, optimizer, schedule, mixture, resolution, sampling)
is our choice. Unlike prior generalists, we target metric depth and analyze why the open recipe falls short
rather than proposing a new architecture.
sections.content: Generative priors for dense prediction. Marigold [18], GeoWizard [9], GenPercept [41], StableNormal [42], and Lotus [14] repurpose diffusion models for depth and normals, mostly predicting relative or affine-invariant 2 Open Vision Banana Fig. 1. Open Vision Banana overview. source image and task instruction pq condition frozen generative backbone (Qwen-Image-2.1 in all experiments; the backbone is configuration choice) that carries one newly initialized rank-64 LoRA adapter δ shared by all tasks. The source enters as visual tokens and reference latents, the instruction as the text condition, and the target latent is generated from noise in 50 flow steps. The generated RGB image ˆrq is converted by parameter-free decoder Dq into structured prediction ˆyq: metric depth, class-ID map, instance masks, or binary mask. Bottom: task contract Cq = (Eq, pq, Dq; Sq) ties encoder, instruction, and decoder to one specification and is validated before training. The scene is rendered illustration; its RGB tiles are produced by the contract encoders from exact annotations and are not model predictions. quantities with task-specific model. StableNormal identifies sampling variance as an obstacle for diffusionbased geometry; we find that in the metric setting this variance concentrates in absolute scale. Specialist metric-depth models reach high zero-shot accuracy with dedicated architectures, large mixed datasets, and often camera intrinsics [2, 4, 20, 25, 34]; OVB uses no intrinsics and no depth head. Referring segmentation. Recent systems couple language model with mask decoder [19, 32, 37] or promptable segmenter [5]; OVB paints the mask as an image with the same adapter that paints depth. Adaptation and weight averaging. OVB trains rank-stabilized LoRA [16, 17] with conditional flow matching [21]. Averaging fine-tuned weights that share an initialization can combine their abilities [39]; we test whether it resolves the task trade-off of shared adapter. What this paper measures. Each failure we report has precedenthard metric scale, sampling variance in diffusion geometry [42], capacity trade-offsso what we establish is their size relative to one another inside one open system, over 42 externally scored checkpoints.

sections.title:
3.3 Training Data and Target Construction
The training pool contains 1,098,435 image–instruction–target records (Fig. 3). Multiple tasks or queries may
share a source image, so these counts describe supervision pairs. Each update samples a task with probability
0.35 for metric depth, 0.20 each for semantic, instance, and referring segmentation, and 0.05 for image-editing
replay; records are sampled uniformly within each task. The replay pool contains 16,492 editing pairs and is
included with the intent of preserving generation ability.
sections.content: The 407,278 depth records combine TartanAir [35], Hypersim [26], LingBot-Depth [30], ARKitScenes [1], SUN RGB-D (excluding NYU-derived samples) [29], and DIODE [31] data. Native-depth admission checks cover 359,693 records, while 47,585 retained legacy records are explicitly exempt from these checks. For newly prepared indoor and DIODE targets, invalid depth pixels are encoded as black; validity masks support data admission but do not mask the training loss. The segmentation pools contain 146,027 semantic and 233,133 instance records, including category-conditioned targets reconstructed from COCONut [7] annotations. In this component, each image contributes one semantic view containing at most 12 eligible classes and up to three category-specific instance views; unselected regions are treated as background relative to the requested categories. Semantic legends use one of four formats, and colors are remapped with probability 0.5 to encourage reliance on the instruction-specified color mapping. Targets are stored as lossless RGB images consistent with the task contracts. The 295,505 referring records comprise 270,195 RefCOCO-family pairs [43], 11,812 Rea2Seg pairs, and 13,498 LLM-Seg COCO pairs. Rea2Seg [12] contributes its GQA, LISA+, and spatial subsets, excluding its ReasonSeg category. LLM-Seg [33] contributes released questions paired with native RLE masks, without answer or chain-of-thought conditioning. Its retained subset is selected through held-out image exclusion, native mask validity and foreground-area checks, and visibility filtering under the 512-pixel training crop. sections.title:
3.4
Inference generates the target from noise with 50 sampling steps, true classifier-free guidance [15] 4.0 against
an empty negative prompt, seed 42, and a 512 × 512 canvas; predictions are decoded and then resized to the
native ground-truth resolution (nearest neighbor for labels, bilinear for depth). Metric depth is scored on
NYUv2 [28] (654 images, Eigen crop [8], 10 m cap), ETH3D [27] (454, 80 m cap), and DIODE-Indoor [31]
(325, no cap) with δ1 and AbsRel accumulated over pixels and without any alignment; we additionally report
a per-image median-aligned δ1 as a diagnostic that uses the ground truth; it corrects a scale but not a shift,
unlike the affine-invariant protocol of [18], and is not comparable to the reference. Cityscapes val [6] (500)
is scored with mIoU over 19 classes from a global confusion matrix, RefCOCOg [23] UMD val [24] (4,896
expressions) with cIoU, and ReasonSeg val [19] (344 queries, original queries, legacy_union masks) with gIoU.
Training and evaluation images are disjoint by image identifier; NYUv2, ETH3D, and ReasonSeg contribute
no training data at all, while DIODE and RefCOCOg contribute their training splits and are reported as
same-source held-out results. All scores come from the same evaluation protocol; per-benchmark details are
in Sec. A.
sections.content: Comparability with the reference. Depth, Cityscapes, and RefCOCOg follow the reference definitions, but the reference does not state crops, caps, aggregation, resolution, or sampling settings, so these are our choices. Two benchmarks are not comparable: Vision Banana rewrites ReasonSeg queries with Gemini 2.5 Pro before segmentation [10], and we pass the original query. We report the reference numbers as context, not as matched comparison.

sections.title:
6 Discussion and Limitations
Implications. The findings translate into three recommendations for generation-as-perception on open models.
(1) Report depth both ways and over seeds. Unaligned scores conflate geometry with an uncommitted scale;
reporting aligned scores and seed spread separates the two. (2) Select checkpoints by decoded metrics. The
flow loss rewards what is easy to reconstruct in latent space, not the global hue that carries scale or the few
regions that decide a mask, so selection needs decoded metrics on a held-out set. (3) Treat scale and task
competition as the targets. Scale can be supervised where it is decided: reconstruct the clean latent from the
predicted velocity, decode it, project onto the cube-edge path, and penalize the per-image log-depth residual.
We provide this optional loss in the released code but have not evaluated it, and make no claim about its
effect.
sections.content: Limitations. Gap to the reference. Our results are below Vision Banana on every benchmark; we do not reproduce its numbers, and its base model, in-house data, and human evaluation are not public. One backbone. The framework supports other generators through configuration, but all findings are on QwenImage-2.1; we do not claim they transfer. Selection on evaluation sets. Checkpoints and merge recipes were inspected on the evaluation benchmarks, so the best reported scores are optimistic by construction: the P5 and P6 weights were fixed after seeing Table 5. Our claims are about the sign of the effect across all six merges, not about any single recipe.

7 Conclusion
We built Open Vision Banana, an open framework in which every perception task is a checked contract
between an RGB encoder, an instruction, and a decoder, and one adapter on a frozen editing backbone serves
all tasks. The open recipe does not match the closed system, but it fails in ways that are now measurable:
depth geometry is nearly right while its absolute scale is uncommitted, segmentation competes with depth for
sections.content: 10 Open Vision Banana shared adapter, weight merging moves along this trade-off without escaping it, and the training loss cannot tell good checkpoints from bad ones. These failure modes, more than any single benchmark number, mark what an open generator must overcome to become generalist vision learner; the released framework and evaluation outputs make each of them testable. The source image is resized so that its area matches 512 512 canvas (side multiple of 32), the target is generated from noise with 50 flow-matching steps and true classifier-free guidance 4.0 against an empty negative prompt, with seed 42. Every raw pipeline output is asserted to be 512 512, and for referring tasks every prompt is asserted to match the instruction template of Tab. 1. The generated image is decoded by the task decoder and the decoded label or depth map is resized to the native ground-truth resolution (nearest neighbor for labels, so that interpolated colors never create phantom classes; bilinear for depth). Metric depth. The decoder projects each pixel onto the cube-edge path and inverts the power transform (Eq. (2)). Valid pixels are those with finite positive ground truth inside the dataset mask, and with finite positive prediction after clipping. NYUv2 uses the Eigen crop and 10 cap, ETH3D an 80 cap, and DIODE-Indoor no cap. AbsRel, RMSE, and δ1 = Pr[max( ˆd/d, d/ ˆd) < 1.25] are accumulated over all valid pixels of the dataset (pixel-weighted), not averaged per image. The aligned diagnostic rescales each predicted map by med(d)/ med( ˆd) over its valid pixels before scoring; it uses the ground truth and is never reported as headline number. Because the prediction-validity filter is applied after decoding, sample that decodes to extreme depths can dominate DIODE AbsRel, which is why we treat DIODE AbsRel as stability indicator. Segmentation. Cityscapes predictions are decoded by nearest palette color, label IDs are mapped to the 19 train IDs, and mIoU is computed from one confusion matrix over the 500 validation images using official gtFine annotations. For referring segmentation, the prediction is thresholded to binary mask; gIoU is the mean IoU over queries, and cIoU is the summed intersection over the summed union. RefCOCOg uses the UMD split (refs(umd).p, 4,896 expressions) with native COCO masks. ReasonSeg uses all 344 queries of the validation set with the original query text and the legacy_union mask rasterization; we also log the official LISA rasterization (lisa_v1), which is 12 points lower. Instance decoder The instance decoder turns one-color-per-instance RGB prediction on black background into binary masks in five stages. The parameters are fixed for every result in this paper. 1. Background initialization. Pixels within Euclidean RGB distance τ = 14 (8-bit scale) of the background color are background. 2. Color grouping. Foreground pixels are grouped by 16-connected, seed-based region growing: pixel joins component when its color lies within τ of the components seed color. The grouping is implemented with unionfind. 3. Noise pruning. Components smaller than θsize = 2 104 of the image area are removed. 4. Boundary-artifact removal. component is removed when 33 erosion keeps less than θerosion = 0. of its pixels, which removes thin halos along instance boundaries. 5. Spatially constrained merging. Two components are merged when their mean colors lie within τ and the bounding box of their union is at most γ = 5 times the sum of their bounding-box areas; merges are applied transitively. The remaining components are the predicted instances; the released code implements the decoder in the SegmentationDecoder class. Fused starting point W0: Melo111/Fusion-C1-KQ0r128-60-40. 18 Open Vision Banana Adapters of runs and B, including every evaluated checkpoint: khazic/ovb-i108-a-lr3e-5-r 64-2x8-s42_20261109r3 and khazic/ovb-i108-b-lr1e-5-r64-2x8-s42_20261109r3. Merges: the merge adapters with their evaluation outputs and SHA-256 checksums, khazic/ovb-i12 7-merge-eval; P6 as standalone BF16 pipeline that needs no adapter, Melo111/Fusion-I108-P6. Evaluation outputs of the main runs: one JSON file per checkpoint and benchmark, with dataset fingerprints and sample counts, khazic/ovb-i120-external-eval. Training data: RefCOCO-family referring targets, Melo111/open-vision-banana-res; depth and reasoning supplements, Melo111/open-vision-banana-depth. Qualitative results Figs. 5 and 6 show predictions of Qwen-Image-2.1 with run at 20k updates (EMA adapter merged into standalone BF16 pipeline, gatilin/ovb-b-20000-best-full) on validation and test images of the evaluation benchmarks; the same samples are shown in the project repository. Depth is shown as the RGB code the model writes, before it is decoded to meters. Instance colors are assigned per instance and need not match the colors of the ground truth, which the decoder does not use. The samples were picked for illustration and are not random draw; the benchmark scores of this checkpoint (row B20k) are in Tab. 8, and those of all checkpoints in Sec. J.
